title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a paycheck that's gone by Thursday, and a hymn that asks fortune not just to come, but to stay

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta asked the fire, Jatavedas, to bring her: make the introduction. What small fire did you keep going? Today, the same request, with one more word, and the end of a week. Day one thousand ninety-two.
screen: `THE SRI SUKTA.` · `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: A paycheck lands on a Friday. By the next Thursday it's mostly spoken for: rent, groceries, a birthday present, the car making that noise again. Money has a way of leaving. It comes in through the front door and slips out the back. Old hymns knew this too. The Sri Sukta has already asked the fire to bring the goddess close. Now it asks again, and adds a small request that sounds almost like a worry. Don't just come. Stay. Today is that one word in the hymn: the one who does not go away.
screen: `IN THROUGH THE FRONT DOOR.` → `OUT THROUGH THE BACK.` → `DON'T JUST COME. STAY.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase. Bring to me, Jatavedas, that Lakshmi who does not go away, in whom I may find gold, cattle, horses, and people. The fire is still the go-between. What's new is the word for her. In Sanskrit it's one long word, anapagamini: the one who does not go away. Notice the honesty in it. You only ask for someone who stays if you know what it is when someone leaves. The hymn admits, near its start, that fortune can come and go. Tradition says it more bluntly elsewhere, calling Lakshmi restless. Here, the singer simply asks. Not for a windfall. A windfall arrives and leaves. He asks for a fortune with roots, a presence that settles into the house. Now look at the list. Gold, cattle, horses, people. In the hymn's world, wealth walks around. It eats. It needs a barn and water and someone up early to tend it. And the last thing on the list isn't a thing at all. People. Some readers hear family there; others hear a household full of helpers and guests. Either way, the hymn counts the faces around the table among the riches. So the line holds a small picture of what staying looks like. Not a pile in a vault. A household that keeps going: animals fed, people gathered, the fire tended. That fits the week behind us. It began with Shakti as a philosophy, the goddess as the power moving through everything. Then the hymn's portrait of gold, silver and moonlight, and the fire asked to make the introduction. Today the request gets specific. Come, and don't go.
screen: `THE FIRE IS STILL THE GO-BETWEEN.` · `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.` · `GOLD, CATTLE, HORSES, PEOPLE.` · `A HOUSEHOLD THAT KEEPS GOING.` · then, large: `COME, AND DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find what stays. Settle, and let the breath come and go on its own. Notice that much first. The breath leaves, and it comes back, without being asked. Then bring to mind one good thing in your life that hasn't gone away. A friend who keeps answering. A habit that holds. A kitchen, a street, a song that's still there. Rest with it, and let the thanks be quiet. If you pray, you can name it before Lakshmi or before God, in the words you already use. If you don't, let the steady thing be enough. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which asks the fire to bring her, and asks for the one who does not go away.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Today, thank one person or thing that has stayed, out loud if you can. Day one thousand ninety-two. A week walked.

howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted by some Hindus in Lakshmi worship at home and in temples, including at Diwali, and some families recite it on Fridays.

original.note: Sanskrit: anapagāminīm, 'the one who does not go away,' Lakshmi in the Sri Sukta.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn asking for money.
what it means: a hymn asking for a fortune that stays, with cattle, horses and people counted among the riches.
what a scholar hears: tāṃ ma āvaha jātavedo lakṣmīm anapagāminīm: Agni as Jatavedas is asked to bring Lakshmi, the one who does not depart.

notes: Review and teach now pick up 1091 (the fire as go-between, avaha) and 1090 (gold, silver, moonlight); the two-readings (plain need vs inner) angle used on 1090 was replaced here with the honesty of asking for one who stays.

Verse 2 paraphrased: tāṃ ma āvaha jātavedo lakṣmīm anapagāminīm / yasyāṃ hiraṇyaṃ vindeyaṃ gām aśvaṃ puruṣān aham. Rendering puruṣān as 'people' (some translate 'men', 'servants', 'sons'); the script says 'some readers hear family, others helpers and guests'. Confirm.
Verse numbering of the Sri Sukta differs between editions (it is a khila hymn appended to the Rig Veda); the script avoids numbering aloud.
Week-end day (1086–1092): the look-back names Shakti as a philosophy (1081–1089) and the Sri Sukta days; confirm with those scripts.
howItsDone: Friday recitation and Diwali use are common practice claims; confirm for wording.
No public-domain English translation quoted; all paraphrase.
'Later stories call Lakshmi restless' (cañcalā) is attributed to later tradition; confirm wording.

Editor pass: the 'later stories call Lakshmi restless, slow to stay where she isn't honored' line was cut back to 'tradition says it more bluntly elsewhere, calling Lakshmi restless' (claims rule: the cited verse doesn't say it); the unsupported 'where she isn't honored' clause dropped.
